questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has a 6 day history of pressure over both cheeks that is worse when she bends forward, a blocked nose, yellow nasal discharge and a reduced sense of smell. It began after a cold. Her temperature is 37.6°C and pulse rate 80 bpm. Both cheeks are tender to percussion.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Facial pressure, congestion, purulent discharge and anosmia after a cold with sinus tenderness is acute rhinosinusitis.

steps.x: Post-viral **facial pain**, **purulent discharge**, congestion and **anosmia** with sinus tenderness.

elim: No itch or seasonal pattern; facial pain and purulent discharge point to sinus inflammation.
Unilateral orbital attacks lasting minutes to hours, not bilateral cheek pressure after a cold.
Localised tooth pain and swelling, not bilateral nasal blockage and anosmia.
No aura, photophobia or nausea; migraine does not cause purulent discharge.

steps.x: **E. Rhinosinusitis.** Facial pain + purulent discharge + congestion after a cold = rhinosinusitis.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man has a 4 day history of nasal congestion, facial pain and green nasal discharge that started with a sore throat and sneezing. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute. There is tenderness over the right maxilla.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
questions.e: Rhinosinusitis is most commonly viral; bacterial infection is secondary and usually later. Green discharge does not prove bacteria.

clues: started with a sore throat and sneezing
steps.x: Early illness that **started like a cold**: the commonest cause is **viral**.

elim: No atopic history or seasonal pattern; it followed a cold.
Seen in immunocompromised patients, not a healthy man after a cold.
Bacterial infection is usually secondary and later; at 4 days most cases are viral.
Possible secondary invader, but green discharge at day 4 does not mean bacteria.

steps.x: **E. Viral infection.** Most rhinosinusitis is viral; bacteria come secondarily.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has his third episode this year of facial pain, nasal blockage and purulent nasal discharge. He smokes 25 cigarettes a day and works as a delivery driver. He has no hay fever and no recent colds. His temperature is 37.3°C. There is tenderness over the left maxilla.
questions.q: Which factor in his history is most likely to predispose him to this condition?
questions.e: Smoking impairs mucociliary clearance and is a recognised risk factor, alongside recent URTI and allergic rhinitis.

clues: no hay fever and no recent colds
steps.x: No URTI and no allergy, so the remaining risk factor is **smoking**.

elim: Not a recognised risk factor in the notes and not in his history.
Not a risk factor for rhinosinusitis.
Not a risk factor for rhinosinusitis.
Not a risk factor; recent URTI, allergic rhinitis and smoking are.

steps.x: **A. Cigarette smoking.** Risk factors: recent URTI, allergic rhinitis, smoking.

questions.stem: A 49 year old woman has had four episodes of facial pain under her eyes with purulent nasal discharge over 8 months. Each settled with treatment but returned. Her temperature is 37.2°C. An ENT specialist arranges imaging of her sinuses.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on CT sinuses?
questions.e: The maxillary sinus is most commonly affected, matching pain under the eyes, so CT shows maxillary opacification.

steps.x: Pain **under the eyes** in recurrent disease: the **maxillary** sinus.

elim: Bony erosion suggests tumour, not recurrent rhinosinusitis.
Frontal involvement gives forehead pain and is less common.
Sphenoid sinusitis is rare and gives deep vertex pain.
She has recurrent disease; CT would show mucosal thickening or fluid.

steps.x: **C. Opacification of the maxillary sinuses.** Maxillary is the most commonly affected sinus.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman has had rhinosinusitis for 9 days. Today her right eye is bulging, the eyelids are red and swollen, moving the eye is painful and her vision is blurred. Her temperature is 38.6°C and pulse rate 108 bpm. Right eye movements are restricted and visual acuity is reduced.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Proptosis, painful restricted eye movements and reduced acuity after sinusitis is orbital cellulitis, not preseptal cellulitis.

steps.x: **Proptosis**, painful **restricted movement** and **reduced acuity**: behind the septum.

elim: Gives a red eye and haloes but not proptosis or restricted movements after sinusitis.
Sticky red eye with normal vision and eye movements.
Lid swelling only; proptosis, painful restricted movements and reduced acuity mean the orbit is involved.
Gradual, not acute with fever after sinusitis.

steps.x: **C. Orbital cellulitis.** Eye signs after sinusitis are a red flag for orbital cellulitis.

questions.stem: A 31 year old man has a 7 day history of a blocked nose, pain over his forehead and cheeks, green nasal discharge and loss of smell after a cold. His temperature is 37.8°C and pulse rate 84 bpm. He is managing at home with paracetamol. He asks which symptoms should make him seek urgent help.
questions.q: Which new feature would most warrant urgent same-day assessment?
o: Visual disturbance such as double vision
questions.e: Eye symptoms, severe headache or neurological signs suggest orbital or intracranial spread and need urgent assessment.

clues: which symptoms should make him seek urgent help
steps.x: Red flags are **eye symptoms**, **severe headache** and **neurological signs**.

elim: Expected in rhinosinusitis; colour does not signal danger.
A typical feature (anosmia), not a red flag.
Prompts consideration of antibiotics, not emergency assessment.
Expected sinus tenderness.

steps.x: **E. Visual disturbance such as double vision.** Eye or neurological symptoms = urgent assessment.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has had a blocked nose, thick nasal discharge, facial fullness and a reduced sense of smell for 5 months. She had several acute episodes of facial pain after colds last winter. Both sides are equally affected and there is no bleeding. Her temperature is 36.9°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Persistent bilateral sinonasal symptoms for months after recurrent acute episodes is chronic rhinosinusitis, a recognised complication.

steps.x: Symptoms for **months** after **repeated acute episodes**, bilateral.

elim: Acute disease lasts under 12 weeks; she has had 5 months of symptoms.
Itch, sneezing and clear discharge, not thick discharge and facial fullness.
Would be unilateral, with bleeding or neck lumps.
Follows overuse of decongestant sprays, which she has not used.

steps.x: **C. Chronic rhinosinusitis.** Chronic sinusitis is a complication of acute rhinosinusitis.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman has a 1 week history of a blocked nose after a cold. Her GP is deciding whether this is rhinosinusitis or allergic rhinitis. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute. Her chest is clear.
questions.q: Which feature would most support rhinosinusitis?
questions.e: Facial pain or pressure with purulent discharge indicates sinus involvement; itch, sneezing and seasonality point to allergy.

steps.x: What makes it **sinus** disease: **facial pain** and **purulent discharge**.

elim: Typical of allergic or viral rhinitis rather than sinus infection.
Points to allergy.
Points to allergic rhinitis.
Typical of allergic rhinitis.

steps.x: **B. Facial pain with purulent discharge.** Sinusitis = facial pain + purulent discharge.

questions.stem: A 37 year old man has an 8 day history of left cheek pain, nasal congestion and a reduced sense of smell after a cold. His temperature is 37.7°C and pulse rate 82 bpm. His GP examines the inside of his nose with an otoscope.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the nasal cavity?
o: Purulent discharge in the nasal cavity
questions.e: Examination in rhinosinusitis shows sinus tenderness and purulent discharge in the nasal cavity.

clues: examines the inside of his nose
steps.x: Acute sinusitis after a cold: look for **pus** in the nose.

elim: Suggests CSF leak, not rhinosinusitis.
Polyps suggest chronic disease, not an 8 day illness.
Follows trauma.
Suggests herpes simplex.

steps.x: **C. Purulent discharge in the nasal cavity.** Exam: sinus tenderness + purulent discharge in the nasal cavity.

questions.stem: A 17 year old boy has had frontal sinus pain and purulent nasal discharge for 2 weeks. Over 3 days he has developed a severe headache, a focal seizure and weakness of his left arm. His temperature is 38.4°C and pulse rate 104 bpm. There is no neck stiffness. Fundoscopy shows papilloedema.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Sinus infection can spread directly through thin bone to the cranial cavity; focal signs and raised pressure suggest a brain abscess.

steps.x: Sinusitis + **focal neurology** + **papilloedema** + fever: a space-occupying infection.

elim: Neck stiffness is absent, and focal weakness with papilloedema suggests a mass.
Does not cause fever, papilloedema or persisting weakness.
Thunderclap onset without preceding sinus infection or fever.
Confusion and seizures, but not after frontal sinusitis with focal mass signs.

steps.x: **B. Brain abscess.** Neurological signs after sinusitis = intracranial complication, think brain abscess.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman had a cold 2 weeks ago. Her nasal symptoms improved, but over 4 days she has developed worsening pain over her right cheek and teeth, thick green nasal discharge and a fever. Her temperature is 38.3°C and pulse rate 96 bpm. The right maxilla is very tender.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her worsening symptoms?
o: Secondary bacterial infection of the sinus
questions.e: Viral inflammation blocks the ostia, so bacteria secondarily infect the sinus, giving worsening after initial improvement.

clues: worsening pain over her right cheek
steps.x: **Improved, then worse** with fever: the **secondary bacterial** phase.

elim: No itch, sneezing or trigger, and allergy does not cause fever.
Tooth pain can occur in maxillary sinusitis; nasal discharge points to the sinus.
She has not used decongestants and this does not cause fever.
Worsening after initial improvement with fever suggests bacteria taking hold.

steps.x: **D. Secondary bacterial infection of the sinus.** Rhinosinusitis is usually viral, with secondary bacterial infection.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man has a 4 day history of facial pain, blocked nose and purulent nasal discharge after a cold. His temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. Both maxillary sinuses are tender. He asks for an X-ray of his sinuses to be sure.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to confirm the diagnosis?
o: Clinical diagnosis from history and examination
questions.e: Rhinosinusitis is a clinical diagnosis; imaging is not needed in uncomplicated acute disease.

steps.x: Typical, uncomplicated, early: **no test needed**.

elim: Reserved for severe or recurrent disease.
Not indicated without red flags.
Does not change management in uncomplicated disease.
Not used; the diagnosis is clinical.

steps.x: **A. Clinical diagnosis from history and examination.** The gold standard is clinical diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has had severe facial pain, nasal obstruction and purulent discharge for 3 months despite intranasal fluticasone, saline irrigation and two courses of antibiotics. He is referred to ENT. His temperature is 37.1°C. Nasendoscopy shows pus in the middle meatus.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate imaging?
questions.e: CT sinuses is the investigation for severe or recurrent rhinosinusitis.

steps.x: **Severe and persistent** despite treatment: image the sinuses.

elim: Used for suspected intracranial complications, not to image sinus anatomy.
Images teeth, not the sinuses.
Poor detail and no longer used.
Not a standard sinus imaging test.

steps.x: **A. CT sinuses.** Severe or recurrent disease: CT sinuses.

questions.stem: A 7 year old girl has had a cold for 9 days with thick yellow nasal discharge, a blocked nose and mild facial pain. She is eating and drinking. Her temperature is 37.6°C and pulse rate 96 bpm. There is pus in both nostrils and no eye swelling. Her mother asks what tests are needed.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: The diagnosis is clinical; a well child with typical rhinosinusitis needs no tests.

steps.x: Well, typical, no red flags: **clinical diagnosis**.

elim: She is not septic.
Only for severe or recurrent disease or complications.
Does not change management in a well child.
Not used in rhinosinusitis.

steps.x: **D. No investigation required.** Rhinosinusitis is diagnosed clinically.

questions.stem: A 15 year old boy has had rhinosinusitis for a week. Since yesterday his left eye has become swollen and pushed forwards, with pain on eye movement and double vision. His temperature is 38.7°C and pulse rate 110 bpm. He is admitted and intravenous antibiotics are started.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to assess the extent of infection?
o: CT of the sinuses and orbits
questions.e: Suspected orbital cellulitis from sinusitis needs CT of the sinuses and orbits to look for abscess and spread.

steps.x: Orbital spread from the sinus: a **CT** shows sinus and orbit.

elim: Does not show whether there is an orbital abscess.
Not the standard test to define sinus and orbital spread.
Too little detail.
Monitors vision but does not image the infection.

steps.x: **A. CT of the sinuses and orbits.** Severe disease or complications: CT sinuses (and orbits).

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman has a 4 day history of facial pain, nasal congestion and yellow nasal discharge after a cold. She has an exam next week and asks for antibiotics. Her temperature is 37.5°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. She is otherwise well.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Paracetamol or ibuprofen and self-care advice
questions.e: Early, mild rhinosinusitis is managed with self-care and simple analgesia; antibiotics are for symptoms beyond 10 days or severe illness.

steps.x: Day 4 and well: **self-care**, no antibiotics.

elim: Antibiotics are not indicated before 10 days unless severe.
For symptoms beyond 10 days or severe illness.
Only for intense flares.
No red flags or structural problem.

steps.x: **D. Paracetamol or ibuprofen and self-care advice.** Mild: paracetamol and ibuprofen.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man has an 8 day history of marked facial pressure, a completely blocked nose and purulent discharge that is stopping him sleeping. Paracetamol and ibuprofen have not helped enough. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 82 bpm. He has no eye or neurological symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Moderate to severe symptoms before 10 days: intranasal corticosteroid with saline irrigation.

steps.x: **Moderate-severe** but under **10 days**: steroid spray.

elim: Antibiotics are for symptoms beyond 10 days or severe illness.
Oral steroids are reserved for intense flares.
No structural problem or unilateral symptoms.
Prolonged use causes rebound congestion.

steps.x: **A. Intranasal fluticasone with saline irrigation.** Moderate-severe: intranasal corticosteroid + saline irrigation.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman with chronic rhinosinusitis uses intranasal fluticasone and saline irrigation daily. Over 2 weeks she has had an intense flare with a completely blocked nose, facial pressure and loss of smell. There is no fever, eye or neurological symptom. Her temperature is 36.8°C. Nasendoscopy shows swollen oedematous mucosa without pus.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional treatment?
questions.e: Oral corticosteroids can be used for intense symptom flares, reducing mucosal oedema.

steps.x: **Intense inflammatory flare** with no infection: systemic steroid.

elim: No sign of bacterial infection.
No pus or fever.
It should be continued.
Rebound congestion with prolonged use.

steps.x: **C. Short course of oral prednisolone.** Oral corticosteroids for intense flares.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has an 11 day history of right facial pain and purulent nasal discharge that is getting worse. He has used paracetamol and intranasal fluticasone. He has no allergies. His temperature is 38.2°C and pulse rate 92 bpm. There are no eye or neurological symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.e: Symptoms beyond 10 days: phenoxymethylpenicillin first-line (NICE NG79).

steps.x: Past **10 days**, no allergy: first-line antibiotic.

elim: Not used for sinusitis in primary care.
Second-line, for worsening on first-line or severe systemic illness.
For penicillin allergy.
Targets staphylococcal skin infection.

steps.x: **E. Phenoxymethylpenicillin.** Beyond 10 days or severe: phenoxymethylpenicillin.

questions.stem: A 10 year old boy has a 12 day history of facial pain and purulent nasal discharge that is not improving. He had a widespread urticarial rash and lip swelling after amoxicillin last year. His temperature is 37.9°C and pulse rate 98 bpm. There are no eye symptoms.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.e: Penicillin allergy: doxycycline in adults, but in a child under 12 clarithromycin is the alternative.

steps.x: **Penicillin allergic** and **under 12**: avoid doxycycline.

elim: A penicillin; he had an allergic reaction.
Contains amoxicillin.
Not used in children under 12 (tooth staining).
A penicillin.

steps.x: **B. Clarithromycin.** Penicillin allergy: doxycycline or clarithromycin.

questions.stem: A 51 year old man has had a blocked nose, reduced sense of smell and thick nasal discharge for 6 months despite daily intranasal fluticasone. His temperature is 36.8°C. Anterior rhinoscopy shows pale grey glistening swellings in both nasal cavities.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Nasal polyps are a structural problem in chronic rhinosinusitis and warrant ENT referral.

steps.x: **Chronic** disease with **polyps**: structural.

elim: Do not treat polyps.
Structural disease needs specialist review.
No acute bacterial infection.
Causes rebound congestion.

steps.x: **C. Referral to ENT.** ENT referral for structural issues or unilateral symptoms.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman has chronic rhinosinusitis with bilateral nasal congestion and occasional facial pressure. Her symptoms are well controlled with daily intranasal fluticasone and saline irrigation. Anterior rhinoscopy shows no polyps and a straight septum. She has no bleeding or one-sided symptoms. She asks to see a specialist.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: ENT referral is only needed for structural issues or unilateral symptoms; well-controlled bilateral disease stays in primary care.

clues: no polyps and a straight septum
steps.x: No polyps, no septal deviation, not unilateral: **no referral**.

elim: Not needed in controlled, non-severe disease.
She has no flare.
Only for structural issues or unilateral symptoms.
No bacterial infection.

steps.x: **A. Continue treatment in primary care.** Refer only if structural or unilateral.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has a 7 day history of facial pain and a blocked nose after a cold. He is started on intranasal fluticasone. His temperature is 37.4°C. His symptoms improve over the next few days and the facial pressure eases.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which the treatment works?
questions.e: Intranasal corticosteroids reduce mucosal inflammation and oedema, opening the ostia and improving sinus drainage.

steps.x: A **corticosteroid**: anti-inflammatory.

elim: That is how decongestants such as xylometazoline act.
Corticosteroids are not antimicrobial.
Antihistamines block H1 receptors; steroids do not.
That is a mucolytic action.

steps.x: **D. Reduces mucosal inflammation and oedema.** Steroid spray reduces oedema and improves drainage.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has recurrent pain over her left cheek with purulent nasal discharge after colds. CT sinuses shows fluid in the left maxillary sinus with a narrow ostium high on its medial wall. The other sinuses are clear. Her temperature is 37.3°C.
questions.q: Which process most directly explains why infection settles in this sinus?
o: Direct spread from the upper teeth
Stasis of secretions behind a blocked ostium
questions.e: The maxillary ostium is narrow and drains against gravity, so it obstructs easily and secretions stagnate.

clues: narrow ostium high on its medial wall
steps.x: **High, narrow** ostium: drains **against gravity**.

elim: No dental disease is described; the CT shows ostial obstruction.
Sinusitis spreads locally, not by blood.
The mucosa is ciliated.
Not a route for sinus infection.

steps.x: **E. Stasis of secretions behind a blocked ostium.** Narrow ostium draining against gravity causes obstruction and stasis.

questions.stem: A 35 year old man develops facial pain and purulent nasal discharge a week after a cold. His temperature is 37.8°C. A medical student asks how a viral cold leads to a sinus infection.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Bony erosion of the sinus wall
questions.e: Viral infection causes mucosal oedema and impaired mucociliary clearance, obstructing the ostia and allowing secondary bacterial infection.

clues: how a viral cold leads to a sinus infection
steps.x: The virus damages the **cilia** and swells the mucosa.

elim: Not part of rhinosinusitis.
Happens in tumours, not post-viral sinusitis.
Allergic rhinitis mechanism.
Oedema reduces ventilation.

steps.x: **D. Impaired mucociliary clearance.** Viral oedema + impaired mucociliary clearance -> ostial obstruction.

questions.stem: A 6 year old girl has rhinosinusitis affecting her ethmoid sinuses. Two days later her right eye becomes swollen and pushed forward with painful eye movements. Her temperature is 38.9°C and pulse rate 128 bpm. CT shows a collection on the medial wall of the orbit next to the ethmoid sinus.
questions.q: Which is the most likely route of spread of infection?
o: Direct spread through the lamina papyracea
questions.e: The thin lamina papyracea separates the ethmoid sinus from the orbit, so infection spreads directly to cause orbital cellulitis.

steps.x: **Medial** orbit next to the **ethmoid**: the paper-thin wall.

elim: Spread is local through bone, not via blood.
Not the route.
Not the route for orbital cellulitis.
Lies posterior; the collection is medial.

steps.x: **A. Direct spread through the lamina papyracea.** Direct spread through thin bone (lamina papyracea).

questions.stem: A 19 year old man had frontal sinusitis 3 weeks ago. He now has fever, headache and drowsiness. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and GCS 13. MRI shows a ring-enhancing lesion in the frontal lobe directly behind the frontal sinus.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of this complication?
o: Direct spread of infection through thin bone
Haematogenous spread from a heart valve
questions.e: Sinus infection spreads directly through the thin bony walls separating the sinuses from the cranial cavity, causing a brain abscess.

steps.x: Abscess **next to** the sinus: contiguous spread.

elim: Not infective.
The lesion lies directly behind the infected sinus.
He has had infection, not a tumour.
Not the typical route.

steps.x: **B. Direct spread of infection through thin bone.** Thin bone separates sinuses from orbit and brain.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man has a 5 day history of nasal congestion, pain behind his eyes and forehead, and a reduced sense of smell after his grandson had a cold. His temperature is 37.7°C and pulse rate 84 bpm. There is purulent discharge in the nose and tenderness over the forehead. There is no neck stiffness.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Rhinosinusitis is inflammation of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses; forehead and retro-orbital pain points to frontal and ethmoid involvement.

clues: pain behind his eyes and forehead
steps.x: Nasal symptoms + **forehead** pain + **anosmia** + pus.

elim: Temporal headache with jaw claudication, not nasal symptoms.
No neck stiffness, rash or photophobia.
Jaw pain on chewing, no nasal symptoms.
Band-like headache with no purulent discharge or anosmia.

steps.x: **A. Acute frontal and ethmoid rhinosinusitis.** Facial pain with nasal symptoms = rhinosinusitis.
